camping-basics-1: I walked light and let the land decide the route, but I never forgot that someone looks after every acre I crossed. Before you pack anything, find out whose ground you mean to sleep on and what the rules are in that place, because they differ across these islands. Pick one site and write down who owns it, who gives permission and what the written rule says. If you cannot answer the question, you are not ready to go there yet. This is the dull part of a trip that makes the rest possible.

The principles are not a list to recite. They are seven questions to put to your own trip. I argued that people who walk through wild places come to care for them, and care shows itself in what you leave behind. Take a real trip you might make and answer each principle in one line: where you will sleep, what you will do with fire, with waste, with water. Where an answer is thin, plan again. The best sign that you have understood is that the plan changes.

Four jobs cause most of the damage: fire, toilet, washing and rubbish. I used dead roots for a fire and fallen needles for a bed, and I could do that because I took little and asked little of the place. You will usually need a good deal more, so take care with each job. Write down what you will do with each of the four, and what you will carry out. Treat fire with the most respect, because it spreads in ways you cannot reverse, and ask whether you need one at all.

Pick a first site that a beginner can be comfortable on, not one that proves anything. A serviced site with a toilet, water and a warden removes the hard questions while you learn the easy ones. Choose it by looking at what it offers and what it does not, and by asking what you would do if the weather turned. Write one sentence on why this site suits this trip. Go simply, take little, and let the first night teach you what the second should be.
camping-basics-2: Size and season decide whether the tent serves you or you serve it. The rating roughly equals the number of sleeping pads that fit on the floor, so for comfort take a size larger than the number sleeping in it. Season ratings tell you how the tent copes with wind and cold, and shape tells you how it will behave in a gale. Pick a tent for a named group and a named trip, and say what you will do about space for bags and boots. A tent that suits the trip is a better choice than one that suits the shop.

Pick the pitch before you take the tent out of its bag. Look for ground that drains and is clear of flood, decide where the wind will come from and where the sun will rise, and never pitch under a dead branch or a shallow-rooted tree. Walk the site and say your reasons aloud. If you cannot defend a choice, move the tent. The ground does more for you, or against you, than any piece of kit you carry.

Practise at home. The worst time to learn is after a long day, in the dark, in the rain. Read the instructions, count the parts, and pack a copy. Pitch in order: footprint, poles, body, fly, then peg out and tension so the fly does not touch the inner. Add guylines when the wind is up. Time yourself pitching it twice in the garden and note what slowed you the first time. A routine you have rehearsed is the one that holds when you are tired.

Condensation is warm air meeting a cold surface, and a tent is full of warm breath. Handle it by site, by keeping moisture out and by moving air through. Pitch away from damp hollows, open the vents, keep wet kit out of the sleeping area and cook outside the inner. Make a short list of the three things you will do at bedtime. You cannot stop the water, but you can stop it from deciding the night.
camping-basics-3: I tested my sleeping gear before I trusted it, and so should you. A bag's rating is an estimate made in a laboratory, not a promise, and your own comfort will not match it exactly. Learn the difference between a comfort figure and a lower limit, and pick the bag by the colder of the two nights you might meet. Write down the figures on your bag and what they mean for your trip. A rating is a starting point, and a test in the garden tells you more than the label.

The ground pulls heat out of you faster than the air does. A pad is as important as the bag, and an air mattress that looks plush may have little insulation. Learn what the R-value means and add pads together when the cold is serious. Build a sleep system on paper: pad, bag, liner, clothes and what goes underneath. Then try it for a night in the garden. If you wake cold, change one thing and try again.

The forecast gives you the air temperature, but the body loses heat to wind, to height and to wet. A bare skin in a breeze feels far colder than the number says. Read the 'feels like' figure as an adjustment, not a separate climate. Plan for the colder conditions you might meet, and know what you will do if you get wet. Write the three ways you lose heat and a control for each.

Go to bed warm and dry, with food in you and dry clothes on. Hypothermia is a drop in body temperature below 35 degrees, and it is a medical emergency. Know the signs: shivering, pale cold skin, slurred speech, slow breathing, tiredness. Rehearse what you will do and whom you will call. Check each other at the end of the day, because a person who is cold often does not notice. Prevention is easier than rescue.
camping-basics-4: Test the stove in the garden before you rely on it. A camp stove can start a fire, trap an escape route, burn you or give off carbon monoxide. Learn the checks before you light it, and how to read the flame once it is lit. Do the sequence aloud, in order, until it is routine. I chose my cooker by the heat it gave for the weight, and I logged what it did; a trial of your own will tell you more than a label.

Carbon monoxide has no colour, taste or smell, and it can build up in a tent awning. Any stove that burns fuel produces some. Cook outside, keep the stove away from the sleeping area, and never use a stove to heat a closed tent. Write down the signs of poisoning and what you will do: get everyone into fresh air and call for help. This is a hazard you cannot detect by your own senses, so you control it by rules.

Clear water can still make you ill. Germs from human or animal waste can reach lakes, rivers and streams, so water from a clear stream is not safe to drink as it is. Choose a method for the germs you are worried about: boiling, a filter, or treatment. Plan how much you need and how you will carry it. Test the method before the trip, and note the time it takes.

Your fridge is a cool box, so plan the food. Take extra care with cooked meat, eggs and dairy, and keep raw and ready-to-eat foods apart in sealed containers. Make a menu for the trip, with what is eaten first and what keeps. I logged the fuel and time each of my cooking tests needed. Do the same: write the menu and the fuel, and wash your hands before you handle food.
camping-basics-5: Before the trip I asked those who knew the ground, and I trusted the map only as far as I could read it. Learn the scale and the key, and measure a distance on the map with string or the compass edge. Plan a short route on paper and say what each symbol tells you. A map is a picture of the ground, so check that the picture matches what you see on the day.

A grid reference says exactly where you are. The blue lines form the National Grid: eastings run up the map and northings run across. Give a four-figure reference and then a six-figure one, and say which square of the map each sits in. Practise on places you know. When you are out, an exact reference is what a rescuer needs, so make the habit before you need it.

A phone can fail, and mist hides everything. A baseplate compass does not run out of power. Take a bearing from the map in four steps, walk it with the needle, and allow for the magnetic variation. Practise on open ground first. I turned back on the plan, not on a feeling, and a bearing is a plan you can follow when you cannot see.

Naismith's rule is a simple estimate: one hour for every five kilometres, plus one hour for every six hundred metres of ascent. Use it to set a turn-back time before you set off, and keep to it. Know the weather limits that change the plan, and write them on your trip card. I accepted that the goal was beyond us and turned back with everyone; a limit set in advance makes that choice easier.
camping-basics-6: Ask three questions before you go: do I have the right gear, do I know the weather, and am I confident in my knowledge and skills? Write the answers on your trip plan. I held that you should check the basic conditions before you guess at a cause, and the same goes for a plan: air, warmth, light, cleanliness, food and who is responsible. If the answer to any question is no, change the plan, not the answer. A plan must also work when you are not there to explain it.

Most harm comes from a short list of hazards. Match each to a control: fire, water, cold, gas, the walk itself. Write the list and the control beside it. Then ask who will do what. A hazard with no named control is still a hazard, and the plan is only as good as the weakest line.

Three illnesses cover the main camp emergencies: cold, gas and dirty water. Each has signs you can see and a response you can give at once. Learn the signs and say them aloud with someone else. Check the basics before you guess at a cause: air, warmth, light, quiet, cleanliness. Observe for a purpose and write down what you see.

When you need help, the order matters. In the hills, dial 999 or 112 and ask for the Police, then Mountain Rescue. Give your prepared details: where you are, how many, what has happened, what you have. Stay where you are until contacted. Practise the call with the details on a card. A calm, complete call is the first step in a rescue.
camping-basics-cap: The brief is a plan, a kit checklist, a trip card and, after the trip, a one-page review. Plan with margins, roles and a turn-back rule, and give someone else the plan. I turned back at a set point because the sums told us to, and the crew came home. Write the plan so a stranger could act on it. Use your own words and cite what you used.

The capstone passes when each rubric row meets its result. Run the trip, keep a log as you go, and afterwards review honestly: what went well, what you would change, what you would do differently next time. Put it in the ledger so the next trip starts from what you learned. A review that names only successes is a poor one.
